**Title:** Which Dollar Broke? Separating Token Failures from Platform-Ledger Failures in Web Dollar Markets

**Abstract (225 words):**

When a crypto exchange loses its banks, the dollars in its customers' accounts can stop being worth a dollar. Those balances are entries in the exchange's own ledger, and they reach bank money only through the platform's banking rails. Web price feeds and on-chain oracles still treat every exchange's USD as the same dollar, so they can report a platform failure as a market move or a stablecoin depeg. Existing work on feed reliability and cross-exchange price gaps does not tell the two apart, and doing so is hard: an exchange's dollar is never quoted on its own, public prices thin out under stress, and any single asset can carry its own shock. We propose a decomposition that prices the platform's dollar through unpegged assets such as BTC against venues whose rails stay open, and accepts the result only when unrelated assets and the venue's internal cross-rates agree. Across banking-rail episodes on three platforms between 2017 and 2023, with stablecoin runs as contrasts, the method attributes the largest dislocations to the platform's ledger rather than to tokens. A filter built on it removes 88% of the hours in which a naive multi-exchange index was off by 100 bps or more, and in one episode the signal appeared months before the loss behind it was disclosed. The findings are descriptive and rely only on public data.

**Suggested keywords:** stablecoins; platform money; exchange ledgers; price feeds and oracles; Web measurement; natural experiment; reproducibility
